corrected_proposal.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing agencies to apply its male/female definitions in federal policy and official communications, remove agency materials it characterized as promoting “gender ideology,” and review grant conditions to prevent funds from promoting that ideology. corrected_proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order titled “Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government.” The order establishes male/female definitions for federal interpretation and official agency business, directs agencies to remove internal and external messages it characterizes as promoting “gender ideology,” and says agencies shall take steps, as permitted by law, to end federal funding of that ideology. It separately directs agencies to assess grant conditions and ensure that grant funds do not promote it; HHS was directed to issue guidance within 30 days. The order also rescinds specified prior executive orders and directs updates on agency implementation within 120 days. Those terms support a narrower account of a signed federal policy directive affecting agency definitions, communications and funding rules. They do not establish that all federal LGBTQ+-specific health programs were terminated on January 20, that CDC HIV surveillance or other health data collection ceased that day, or that crisis hotlines ended. The supplied original's claims about those outcomes, named programs and immediate effects are not stated in the order. This entry records the order's text and scope; implementation and downstream effects require separate evidence.

corrected_proposal.description_short: A June 4 proclamation suspended entry for some incoming Harvard students and only called for discretionary review of current visas.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On June 4, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation suspending entry for certain nonimmigrant students seeking to begin study at Harvard through SEVP, with exceptions and a stated six-month duration. It separately directed the Secretary of State to consider whether some current Harvard students’ visas should be revoked. That instruction did not establish that current students’ visas had already been canceled. A later temporary court order blocked the policy, according to Harvard Gazette.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On June 4, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a proclamation suspending entry for nonimmigrants seeking to begin a course of study at Harvard through the Student and Exchange Visitor Program. The proclamation set a six-month period unless extended and included exceptions; it also said the restriction did not apply to students entering to attend other universities through the program. Separately, it directed the Secretary of State to consider, in the Secretary’s discretion, whether certain current Harvard students with F, M, or J visas should have them revoked. That wording authorized a review; it does not say that visas belonging to dozens of current students had already been canceled. The proclamation stated national-security concerns and alleged Harvard had failed to provide records about foreign students. Harvard Gazette reported that University officials denied that allegation and that DHS had moved in May to pull Harvard’s certification. The Gazette also reported a temporary court order issued June 5 blocking the administration’s plan. This supported entry covers the June 4 proclamation and separates it from the earlier certification dispute and April SEVIS record terminations. The number of students affected by those separate actions remains unresolved.

ABC also notes that justices decide for themselves when recusal is appropriate.

The supplied entry’s February 2025 date and reference to Ketanji Brown Jackson do not match the documented event: the source identifies Ruth Bader Ginsburg and dates the demand to February 25, 2020. The source supports a recusal demand and an accusation of unfair treatment; it does not support the separate claim that Trump accused the justices of racism. corrected_proposal.title: Justice Department Seeks to Terminate Flores Protections for Detained Children
corrected_proposal.description_short: Justice Department Seeks to Terminate Flores Protections for Detained Children
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On May 22, 2025, the Justice Department, DHS, and HHS filed a motion asking a federal court to terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement and dissolve an injunction covering agency regulations. The agreement sets protections for minors in immigration custody, including limits on detention and basic care standards. A federal judge denied the termination request in August, so the protections were not ended by this motion.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On May 22, 2025, the Justice Department, acting with the Departments of Homeland Security and Health and Human Services, asked a federal court to terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement and dissolve an injunction covering agency regulations. The 1997 agreement sets protections for children in immigration custody, including limits on detention and requirements for adequate food, water, and clean clothes. The filing argued that changed circumstances and agency regulations made continuation inequitable; that was the government’s position, not a court finding. The motion sought to end the settlement’s protections, but the request was not itself an effective termination. In August 2025, the district court denied the motion, saying the defendants had not identified new facts or law that warranted ending the agreement. This repaired entry records the government’s attempt to terminate court-supervised protections, with the correct May filing date and the distinction between a request and an enacted change. The February claim that the administration had already rescinded multiple agreements or eliminated independent oversight is not supported by these records. The later denial confirms that the Flores agreement remained in effect after this motion.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
U.S. District Court for the Central District of California

The parties agreed to a filing date of May 22, 2025, opposition on June 20, 2025, reply on July 3, 2025, and hearing on July 18, 2025.

Defendants move to terminate the FSA under paragraph 40 of the FSA and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(4), (b)(5), and (b)(6).

source_fact_map.fact: The federal district court denied the motion to terminate in August 2025.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Before the Court is Defendants’ Motion to Terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement and to Dissolve the Court’s 2019 Injunction. The motion is fully briefed. The Court held a hearing on the motion on August 8, 2025. Defendants fail to identify any new facts or law that warrant the termination of the Flores Settlement Agreement at this time. Therefore, for the reasons set forth below, the Court DENIES Defendants’ MTT.

source_fact_map.fact: The government motion also asked the court to dissolve its injunction of agency regulations.

insight_facts: On May 22, 2025, federal defendants moved to terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement and dissolve the court's injunction.
The Flores agreement set detention and basic-care protections for children in immigration custody.
The court denied the termination motion in August 2025.

evidence_map.fact: The Flores agreement limits detention time for children and requires basic care including adequate food, water, and clean clothes.
The departments agreed to a May 22, 2025 filing date, and defendants moved to terminate the Flores Settlement Agreement.
The federal district court denied the motion to terminate in August 2025.
The government motion also asked the court to dissolve its injunction of agency regulations.
